newsitem.title: FRANCE: French politicians fire first shot in euro-dlr war.
newsitem.headline: French politicians fire first shot in euro-dlr war.

text.p: French politicians have fired the first shot in what may be a long war over exchange rate policy and, in doing so, revived questions about whether France and Germany share the same vision of their future common currency.

Economists and officials say renewed debate in France about its decade-old strong franc policy is really a discussion about how Europe should manage the euro-dollar exchange rate after 1999, amid fears Germany will insist on a strong euro.
France has said repeatedly the dollar is undervalued, whereas in Germany, memories of 1930s hyperinflation make the idea of letting the euro be a weak currency anathema.
"We are having the beginnings of a debate of what will happen after the European single currency comes together," UBS economist Darren Williams said.

There is little sign yet that those doubting current policy -- doubts expressed this week even by some members of the Bank of France, traditional guardian of monetary orthodoxy -- are gaining the upper hand.

But they are nonetheless tapping into a vein of tension between Germany and France over exchange rates, which is stoking criticism of France's decade-old policy of keeping the franc level-pegging with the mark even as it rose against the dollar.

"I don't think that what we have now is a debate about whether we want to link our future to Germany or not. The thing now is a problem of how strong the euro will be," Daiwa Institute of Research economist Bernard Godement said.
"I have the feeling that there is a major policy conflict with Germany," he said.

The official line is that the exchange rate between the dollar and the euro will matter much less after European Economic and Monetary Union since the vast bulk of trade will be inside Europe and therefore inside the euro zone.
"Our commercial transactions will be sheltered from currency fluctuations," a senior finance ministry source said.
"What is very urgent is to switch to the euro," the finance ministry source said.

And, the theory goes, as the euro gains credibility, becoming a rival reserve currency to the dollar, the United States will find it harder to get away with a weak currency without paying the price in terms of higher interest rates.

"This undervaluation of the dollar boosted the American economy which also enjoys a unique privilege, due to the United States' role as a world leader," Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean Boissonnat said in an article published last Sunday.
"When the dollar weakens, America does not pay the cost in interest rates, as is the case in any other country," he wrote in weekly Le Journal du Dimanche.

Lining up against that view, however, is an increasingly vocal minority arguing that France desperately needs a change of policy to cut unemployment, already running at a record 12.6 percent and expected to keep rising.
"The way things are going the present conservative majority could very well lose the (1998 parliamentary) election," Godement said.
A debate which already appeared to be rumbling under the surface for some time burst into the open last week when ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a sharp depreciation in the franc.

And in rare public comments from the secretive inner sanctum of the Bank of France, two members of its nine-member policy council broke ranks from its traditional cautious line, calling for faster easing in interest rates.
It was the first sign Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet, nicknamed the Ayatollah of the strong franc, had any difficulties ensuring the council toed the line.
In a statement on Friday, Trichet said he was the only person qualified to speak for the central bank and said other council members spoke in a purely personal capacity.
The government meanwhile has said it will press its argument for a rise in the dollar with its partners in the Group of Seven rich nations.

The fact that the United States is now beginning to take monetary union seriously, and seek reassurance that the euro will be as strong a currency as the mark now is, may be the proof France's leaders are looking for that the move to EMU will improve Europe's bargaining power on exchange rates.
